beats.say: Finance has a sales table of 40 terabytes.
Every monthly report scans all of it. And costs a fortune.
beats.label: The pain
beats.head: Every report scans everything

beats.say: The goal: scan gigabytes, not terabytes. Three ideas do it.
beats.label: Station 3.2 · The data warehouse
beats.head: Scan gigabytes, not terabytes

check.prompt: In BigQuery, where do the order lines best live?
options: In a separate table, joined each time
Inside the order row, as a repeated field
In a CSV file in a bucket
check.why: Nested and repeated fields keep data that is read together in one row. No join is needed.

beats.say: First: how you shape the tables.
App databases normalize. Every fact is stored once, in many small tables.
beats.label: App databases
beats.head: Normalize: many small tables

beats.say: BigQuery likes the opposite. Storage is cheap. Joining huge tables is not.
beats.label: BigQuery
beats.head: Denormalize: joins are the cost

beats.say: So keep the order lines inside the order row, with nested and repeated fields.
beats.label: The BigQuery way
beats.head: Nested and repeated fields
beats.text: STRUCT and ARRAY: no join needed

beats.say: Data that is read together is stored together.
beats.label: In one line
beats.head: Read together, stored together

check.prompt: Reports always filter by date, and often by customer ID. Which design is best?
options: Partition by date, cluster by customer ID
check.why: Partition on the date filter. Cluster on the column with many values.

beats.say: Second, and the big one: partitioning.
Think of a filing cabinet with one drawer per day.
beats.label: Think of a cabinet
beats.head: One drawer per day

beats.say: Ask for last week, and BigQuery opens seven drawers. It never touches the rest.
beats.label: Pruning
beats.head: Open 7 drawers, skip the rest

beats.say: So partition on the date you filter by.
beats.label: The rule
beats.head: Partition on the date you filter by

beats.say: Clustering sorts the data inside each drawer, by up to four columns.
beats.label: Clustering
beats.head: Sorted inside each drawer

beats.say: Use it for columns with many values, like customer ID.
beats.label: When to cluster
beats.head: Cluster on high-cardinality columns

beats.say: The best setup uses both. Partition by date, then cluster by your common filters.
beats.label: Combine them
beats.head: Partition by date + cluster by filter

beats.say: The trap: partitioning on an ID column. Cluster on it instead.
beats.label: Exam trap

beats.say: Third: views.
A normal view is a saved query. It runs again every time.
beats.label: Logical view
beats.head: A saved query. Runs every time.

beats.say: A materialized view stores the answer, and keeps it fresh. Great for repeated totals.
beats.label: Materialized view
beats.head: Stores the answer, keeps it fresh

beats.say: To change a column's type, rebuild the table with create or replace table, as select.
beats.label: Change a type
beats.text: CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE … AS SELECT CAST(…)

beats.say: Recap.
Denormalize with nested fields. Partition on your date filter. Cluster on busy columns.
beats.label: Station 3.2

beats.say: Now make that report cheap. Checkpoint below.
